use_case.name: Early warning for delinquent accounts
use_case.summary: A weekly list of contracts likely to go 30+ days past due in the next 60 days, so collections can call early and offer a payment plan. Outreach priority only: it doesn't change credit terms, limits or pricing.

intake.problem: Trouble shows up only at the first missed payment, when the equipment may already be idle, moved or sold.
intake.who: Collections team under Tom Brandt; 11,000 active contracts.
intake.today: Collections works accounts by days past due; a senior analyst keeps a gut-feel watchlist from industry news and utilization reports.
intake.volume: 11,000 active contracts; 6.2% went 30+ days past due last year.
intake.cost: $9.8M net charge-offs last year (0.70% of the portfolio). Early contact cuts losses on an account by about a third (collections estimate).
intake.wrong_answer: A miss is what happens today; a false alarm is a polite call to a good customer. Collectors decide every action.
intake.data: Seven years of payment history in servicing (lands nightly in Snowflake); origination data in a separate system, not in Snowflake; telematics for about 40% of the fleet. Customer IDs don't always match after a 2021 re-key; industry codes often blank; financials updated yearly at best. Sole-proprietor names, tax IDs, emails and phones.
intake.sign_off: Tom Brandt (owner), Helen Mbeki (sponsor), security, compliance, warehouse-line banks.

input.evidence: Structured data: payment history, days past due, amounts, codes, engine hours.

rules.evidence: Nobody can write down rules for spotting trouble before a miss: days-past-due rules fire only after one, and the analyst's watchlist is unwritten judgment.

output.evidence: A probability of 30+ days past due within 60 days, per contract.

alternative.evidence: Rules on payment-date drift, partial payments and utilization drops would catch some early cases, perhaps half.

alternative.description: A rule-based watchlist: flag contracts whose payments arrive later each month, that make partial payments, or whose engine hours drop sharply. Build it first as the baseline; the model ships only if it clearly beats these rules in the back-test.

value.evidence: Net charge-off rate, 0.70% last year ($9.8M), target 0.55%.

volume.evidence: 11,000 active contracts, a 6.2% 30+ day rate and $9.8M in net charge-offs, all from the servicing system.

owner.evidence: Tom Brandt owns collections and the outcome; the CFO sponsors it.

wrong_answer.evidence: A false alarm costs one courtesy call; collectors decide every action; the list never changes terms.

availability.evidence: Seven years of payment history exist, but origination data isn't in the warehouse, telematics covers about 40% of the fleet, and the two systems don't share a reliable customer key.

quality.evidence: Profile of the 1,200-row sample: origination_customer_id 17.8% empty, industry_code 22.8% empty, financials_as_of 31.3% empty and newest 300 days old, contract_id has 4 repeated values. Repeats in servicing_customer_id are expected (several contracts per customer).

access.evidence: Owners are named (Tom Brandt for servicing, Ravi Shah for origination). Servicing lands in Snowflake nightly; origination has no read path yet.

sensitivity.evidence: The profile flags owner names, tax_id, contact_email and contact_phone. The team knows what's there but has no masking plan yet.

regulations: ECOA and Regulation B (fair lending, including business credit)
FCRA, if credit bureau data is used as a feature
GLBA safeguards for customer financial data
State privacy laws for sole proprietors

sign_off.needs: Data flow from servicing and origination into Snowflake, masked views for the model, where training and scoring run, and who can see the weekly list.
The feature list with a review for proxies of protected classes, proof that the list only orders outreach, and that every flagged customer is offered the same plan options.
Model documentation: data sources, the back-test against the rule baseline, validation, monitoring and drift checks.

sign_off.who: Tom Brandt and Ravi Shah, data owners
sign_off.needs: Which tables and fields, read-only access, and sign-off on the customer ID crosswalk.
The charge-off metric, baseline, target and check date.

reasons: Predicting which current accounts will go late is a forecast from many weak signals, and the existing days-past-due rules only fire after the miss. It passes the Simplicity Test (5 of 8) but not by much, so a rule-based watchlist is the baseline to beat.
The value is clear and large: net charge-offs were $9.8M last year, and there is a named owner, a sponsor, and a cheap cost for false alarms.
The data exists and has owners, but it isn't ready (4 of 8): origination isn't in the warehouse, customer IDs don't match after the 2021 re-key, and key fields are 18% to 31% empty in the sample.
These are weeks of data work, not a research problem. Fix them first, then build; building on the broken join would train the model on mismatched customers.

top_risks.risk: The model doesn't beat a simple drift-and-partial-payment rule.
top_risks.mitigation: Back-test both on the same months; ship the rules if the model doesn't clearly win.

top_risks.risk: Features such as state or industry act as proxies for protected classes, creating fair-lending exposure even in collections.
top_risks.mitigation: Compliance reviews the feature list before training; direct identifiers stay out; every flagged customer gets the same plan options; results are documented for the banks.

top_risks.risk: Crosswalk mistakes attach the wrong origination data to a customer.
top_risks.mitigation: Build the crosswalk with a match confidence, have both data owners review it, and leave unmatched contracts out of training.

first_build.scope: After the data fixes: a model trained on servicing history plus crosswalked origination data, back-tested on the first half of 2026 against the rule baseline. If it wins, a weekly top-200 list for two collectors for eight weeks.
first_build.left_out: Telematics (40% coverage, next version), annual financial statements as features, any automatic action, and any change to terms, limits or pricing.

measure.target: 0.55% annualized, with the roll rate to 30+ days past due among flagged accounts reviewed monthly from the first list

data_fixes.owner: IT data team with Ravi Shah
data_fixes.done_when: Origination tables load nightly with a freshness check.

data_fixes.gap: Customer IDs don't match between origination and servicing (17.8% blank in the sample, plus re-keyed IDs).
data_fixes.done_when: A reviewed crosswalk matches at least 98% of active contracts.

data_fixes.gap: contract_id repeats in the extract (4 in 1,200 rows).
data_fixes.done_when: contract_id is unique in the extract.
Under 5% blank on active contracts, or blanks are an explicit "unknown" the model can use.

data_fixes.gap: Tax IDs and owner contact details sit next to the features.
data_fixes.owner: IT security and the data team
data_fixes.done_when: The model reads a masked view with no direct identifiers.

result.human_review: A person reviews every output in the first build.
